title.en: Gawigawen of Adasin: The Three-Nosed Husband and the Bride Who Became Oil
title.zh: 阿達辛的加維加溫：三鼻夫與化油的婚娘

region.en: Natpangan and Adasin (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省納特潘甘與阿達辛（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode, pp. 58-61

summary.en: Gawigawen of Adasin asks his mother Dinawagan to arrange his marriage with the sister of Aponibalagen; the balaua is filled eighteen times with valuable things, the spring's sand is beads, and Aponibalagen beheads old Taodan to make a spring and a shade-tree for the bride. But Aponibolinayen, told by Indiapan that her husband has three noses, keeps her face covered, melts to oil every night — and on the fifth night drops herself away into the jungle, where a rooster and a monkey both tell her Indiapan lied because she wanted to marry Gawigawen herself.
summary.zh: 加維加溫託母親迪納瓦甘說親；聘禮十八次填滿巴勞瓦，泉邊金沙如珠。為討新娘歡心，阿波尼巴拉根斬老者陶丹之首化泉成蔭。但新娘被英迪亞潘告知『夫有三鼻』，始終以手遮面、夜夜化為油；第五夜她悄然棄身而遁，入密林——雄雞與巨猿皆言：英迪亞潘只因自己想嫁加維加溫，故出此謊。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The head taken to make the spring is placed on the sagang; the balaua and pakdlon ceremonies are named, not described operationally.

passages.text: 'Mother Dinawagan, go and engage me to someone, for I want to be married. I like the sister of Aponibalagen of Natpangan,' said Gawigawen of Adasin. His mother took her hat which looked like the moonbeam and started; when she arrived in Natpangan, Ebang broke up the fish stick and put it in the pot and it became fish, and they drank from the basi jar which was nine times inherited before Dinawagan said, 'My son Gawigawen of Adasin wants to marry your sister.' Aponibalagen agreed, so she gave a golden cup which looked like the moon as an engagement present, and they agreed on a day for pakdlon. When all whom they had invited arrived they agreed how much Gawigawen should pay for his wife: Aponibalagen told them to fill the balaua eighteen times with valuable things — so the balaua was filled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the spring of Gawigawen of Adasin they were surprised, for it was very beautiful and its sands were of beads, and the grass they used to clean pots with was also beads, and the place where the jars sat was a big dish. 'Go and tell Gawigawen that he must come here and bring an old man, for I am going to take his head and make a spring for Aponibolinayen,' said Aponibalagen. So someone went and told Gawigawen to bring the old man Taodan with him to the spring; Aponibalagen cut off his head and he made a spring, and the water from it bubbled up and the body became a big tree called Alangigan which used to shade Aponibolinayen when she went to the spring to dip water, and the blood of the old man was changed to valuable beads. The place where they walked, from the spring to the ladder of the house, was all big plates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: Aponibolinayen covered her face all of the time and sat down in the middle of the house, for Indiapan said that she must not uncover her face, for her husband Gawigawen had three noses, and she was afraid to look at him — but Gawigawen was a handsome man, and Aponibolinayen believed what Indiapan had told her. Not long after Dinawagan spread the string of agate beads along the floor where Aponibolinayen sat; when Gawigawen went to Aponibolinayen at night she changed to oil, and she did that every night, and they put the carabao hides under her mat so the oil would not drop to the ground. On the fifth night she used magic so that they could not see her go out: she dropped her beads under the house, then she became oil and dropped her body, and so she went away, always walking, while Gawigawen looked for her for a long time and went to Natpangan, for he could not find her in any of the towns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Aponibolinayen was in the middle of the jungle she met a wild rooster which was crowing: 'Where are you going, Aponibolinayen? Why are you walking in the middle of the jungle?' — 'I came here, for I am running away from my husband, for I do not want to be married to him, for he has three noses.' 'No, Gawigawen is a handsome man. I often see him, for this is where he comes often to snare chickens. Do not believe what Indiapan said to you, for she is crazy,' said the rooster. Aponibolinayen walked on until she reached the place of many big trees, and the big monkey met her: 'Why don't you wish to marry Gawigawen?' — 'Because Indiapan told me he has three noses.' The monkey laughed and said, 'Do not believe that. Indiapan wants to marry Gawigawen herself. He is a handsome man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Gawigawen of Adasin' episode; not verbatim.

title.en: Kadayadawan and the Carabao: The Bride Found Across the Ocean
title.zh: 卡達雅達萬與水牛：越洋尋得的新娘

region.en: Pintagayan and Natpangan (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省平塔加揚與納特潘甘（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale, told by Magwati of Lagangilang; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode, pp. 61-64

summary.en: Aponibolinayen, fleeing her three-nosed husband, rides a carabao across the ocean to an orange tree; the carabao fetches Kadayadawan of Pintagayan — 'there is a good toy for you' — who wins her when their betel-quids become agate beads. At the balaua Gawigawen seizes her into his belt during the dance and Kadayadawan spears him down and revives him; the alan who raised Kadayadawan reveals he was picked up as blood that fell from Langa-an — so he is re-named Aponitolau, the marriage price repaid, and a golden house flies to Kadalayapan.
summary.zh: 逃離三鼻丈夫的阿波妮波莉納衍，騎水牛渡海至橘樹下；水牛喚來平塔加揚的卡達雅達萬——『給你尋了個好玩具』。兩人檳榔渣化為瑪瑙珠，遂成婚。塞揚宴上，加維加溫於舞中將她收進腰帶；卡達雅達萬擲矛擊倒他、復又救活。養育他的阿蘭揭示：他原是朗嘉安失血所化——遂得新名阿波尼托勞；金屋一夜飛抵卡達拉雅潘。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative told by Magwati of Lagangilang; collected 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. The belt-seizure incident 'is frequently found in these tales; it also occurs in Javanese literature' (Cole); the alan are lesser spirits.

passages.text: Not long after she reached a wide field, and she did not know where she was; she stopped in the middle of the field, and she thought she would go on to the other side. Not long after she reached the ocean and she sat down on a log, and a carabao came along; it passed often where she sat, and Aponibolinayen thought she would ride on the carabao, and she got on its back and it took her to the other side of the ocean. When they reached the other side Aponibolinayen saw a big orange tree with much fruit on it. The carabao said, 'Wait here while I eat grass and I will return soon' — but the carabao went to the place of the man who owned him and said, 'Come over here, for there is a good toy for you.' So he combed his hair and oiled it and put on his striped coat and his clout and belt, and he took his spear and rode on the carabao's back — and when they reached the orange tree, Aponibolinayen looked down and saw a handsome man. 'Good morning, lady,' he said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long after they chewed betel-nut and they told their names: 'My name is Kadayadawan of Pintagayan, who is the son of an alan.' 'My name is Aponibolinayen of Natpangan, who is the daughter of Pagbokasan and Ebang, who is the sister of Aponibalagen.' Their betel-nut quids became agate beads, and Kadayadawan said to her, 'Ala, it is good for us to marry. I am going to take you home.' So he took her to his home and he was good to his carabao, because it had found him a pretty woman. When they reached the house the Ati commanded the soldiers to call Kadayadawan — the king said, 'Why, Kadayadawan, have you a pretty girl in your house? Every night I notice that your house appears as if it were burning' — 'No, I have not,' answered Kadayadawan; 'I think you have, for I notice the flames every night.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he reached home Aponibolinayen said to him, 'It is best for us to make Sayang' — and Kadayadawan asked how they could make Sayang by themselves, their neighbors being all soldiers; but Aponibolinayen used magic so that when she thrust the molave stick in the ground it became a balaua, and the betel-nuts they oiled went to the towns of their relatives to invite them. The betel-nut that arrived in Natpangan said to Aponibalagen, 'We came to call you, for Kadayadawan of Pintagayan is making balaua' — 'How can we attend the balaua when we are searching for my sister?' — 'If you do not wish to come I will grow on your knee' — 'Go on my pig' — and the betel-nut grew on the pig until it squealed; 'Ala, get off from the pig and we will come.' At the river Kadayadawan used his power so that their old clothes, which they wore in mourning for Aponibolinayen, were taken off from them, and they were surprised, for they did not know when their old clothes had been taken off; he brought clothes for them, and urged them until they accepted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon they reached the town and they danced; Iwaginan made Gawigawen and Aponibolinayen dance, and while they were dancing Gawigawen watched Aponibolinayen, and when they had danced around nine times Gawigawen seized her and put her in his belt. 'Why do you do that, Gawigawen?' said Kadayadawan to him, and he threw his spear and Gawigawen fell down, and Aponibolinayen escaped, and Kadayadawan put her in a room; as soon as he put her in the room he went to bring Gawigawen back to life. 'Why did you do that, Gawigawen? I did not steal Aponibolinayen from you.' 'Even if you did steal Aponibolinayen from me, she was my wife and I could not find her until now. That is why I put her in my belt, and Aponibalagen knows that she is my wife.' 'She is my wife now.' Not long after, the alan who took care of Kadayadawan told Langa-an, 'Kadayadawan is your son. I picked him up when he was only blood which fell from you' — and they were very happy; they paid the marriage price, filled the balaua nine times with valuable things, repaid Gawigawen what he had paid when he married Aponibolinayen, and took Kadayadawan home as Aponitolau, the alan giving all her things and flying to the other part of the world while Langa-an used magic so that the golden house which the alan gave went to their town of Kadalayapan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Kadayadawan and the Carabao' episode; not verbatim.

title.en: Aponibolinayen Goes to War: Ginambo of Gonigonan
title.zh: 阿波妮波莉納衍出征：貢尼貢南的金南波

region.en: Kaodanan and Gonigonan (Tinguian mythic towns), Abra Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋阿布拉省卡奧達南與貢尼貢南（丁桂安神話城鎮，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tinguian oral epic-cycle tale; collected 1903-1908, published 1915 (Fay-Cooper Cole)

source.work: Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian: A Study in Philippine Folk-Lore (Field Museum, 1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes, pp. 64-69

summary.en: Ginambo of Gonlgonan comes to carry off Aponibolinayen 'whom we do not like'; her father would go in her place, but she refuses — 'you are weak.' On a high rock she glances off their spears like rain and charms her own: spear, kill six and seven at one time; headaxe, cut off their heads from the left and right, from in back and in front. She spares Ginambo alone, agreeing to fight in her town next month; meeting Aponigawani on the road — her quid covered with gold to the other's agate — they go to war together, their invisible helpers summon the brothers Lingiwan and Dangdangayan, who scoop the 'girls who never go out of the house' into their belts.
summary.zh: 金南波率眾來劫『不喜歡的女子』；父親欲代戰，阿波妮波莉納衍拒之——『你太弱了。』她立於高岩，以肘格開雨點般的飛矛，再施咒於己器：矛一擲殺六七人；斧左右前後皆能取首。她獨赦金南波，約下月再戰；途中遇同樣出戰的阿波妮加瓦妮——檳榔渣一金一瑪瑙——二人結伴出征，隱形靈使喚來其兄弟林基萬與當當加揚，將『足不出戶的姑娘』攬入腰帶。

sensitivity.note: Tinguian epic-cycle narrative recorded 1903-1908 by Fay-Cooper Cole; archival record. Head-taking and head poles (sagang) are part of the narrative world; the lala-am ('those within') are the sheltered girls. The betel-quid omen (gold vs agate) marks relative power.

passages.text: There was a woman whose name was Ginambo of Gomgonan, who went to fight Aponibolinayen of Kaodanan; when she reached the place where the spring was she said, 'You people who are dipping water from the spring, whose place is this where the spring is?' — 'It belongs to Aponibolinayen of Kaodanan.' When they went up to the town they raised a clamor: 'There are many women who have come to fight against you, at the place where the spring is.' Aponibolinayen hurried to take her spear. 'Do not go, Aponibolinayen, for I will go,' said her father Pagatipanan; 'No, for you are weak. What can you do now? Once you did kill people in the place where the spring is, and now perhaps it is my fortune.' She went to the spring, and looked down — and truly the enemies looked like many locusts about the spring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ginambo of Gonlgonan said, 'You people who live with me, you are anxious to carry away this woman whom we do not like' — 'Yes, but only our names will go back to the towns we came from,' they answered, i.e. they expected to be killed. Aponibolinayen said, 'You old enemy, take this betel-nut,' and she cut it in two and gave it to them. 'Ala, now do what you can,' shouted Aponibolinayen, who stood on a high rock; when they started toward her their spears looked like rain, they were so many, and she glanced off the spears with both elbows. 'Now I am the next to throw my spears,' said Aponibolinayen. She said, 'I will use my magic, and you, my spear, shall kill six and seven at one time, and you, my headaxe, cut off their heads from the left side and from the right side, and in back and in front.' 'Ala, you spare me so that I may tell the people in Gonigonan where I live,' said Ginambo; 'Yes, but next month I will come to your town Gonigonan to fight,' said Aponibolinayen — and Ginambo went home alone to her town, for all her companions were lost, because they did not throw their spears at Aponibolinayen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon after that Ginawan of Nagtinawan said, 'Let us go to fight Aponigawani of Kadalayapan' — 'No, we do not wish to go, because the people who live in Kadalayapan are powerful like Kaboniyan' — 'No, we go,' said Ginawan. When they reached the spring at Kadalayapan, the women who dipped water said, 'We do not know who is the bravest, whom we should tell, for Aponigawani has no brother.' Then Aponigawani was in a hurry to go: 'Do not go, you will kill somebody,' said her father; 'No, father, the spring will be lost and then what can we do? Father, I am a woman and since I have no brother, perhaps it is my fortune to fight, for you are weak.' She took her skirt, headaxe, and spear and went to the edge of the hill above the spring, where the enemies were thick like locusts about the well; she stood on a high stone with her hands on her hips while they threw their weapons — 'Now, I am next: You, my spear, when I throw you, kill at once seven and six; and you, my headaxe, cut off their heads from the left and right sides, from in back and in front' — until Ginawan begged, 'Please, my friend, let me live so that someone may go back to the town we came from.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.

passages.text: Bye and bye Aponibolinayen, walking in the middle of the road, stopped because she was tired, and Aponigawani, also walking, looked up and saw a woman to whom none compared, and was startled: 'Here is a woman who looks like me.' They leaned their spears together between them and then talked; 'Ala, let us chew betel-nut' — and the quid which had been chewed by Aponigawani was covered with agate beads which are called pinogalan, and the quid of Aponibolinayen was covered with gold. 'You are more beautiful and have more power than I, because your betel-nut is covered with gold,' said Aponigawani. They told their names — both going to war for the agreed month — and went first to Gonigonan, then to Nagtinawan, their invisible helpers flying to summon Dangdangayan of Naglitnan and Lingiwan of Nagtangpan. When the two men arrived they looked into the town and saw the two women who looked like flames of fire, because of their beauty; the people whom they killed were so many that the pig troughs floated in their blood, and Dangdangayan went in front of the women and scooped them up with his headaxe and put them inside of his belt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.

passages.text: They went home and sent all the heads before them and also the plunder, and carried the women inside of a big jar. 'Why, Aponibolinayen is here and Lingiwan also,' they said at Kaodanan; Dingowan of Nagtangpan took Aponibolinayen and put her inside of a big jar. At the balaua that followed, old Pagbokasan took Aponibolinayen from the jar and put her inside of his belt; and when they chewed the betel-nut covered with gold to see if the two young men who took home Aponigawani were their relatives, the spittle of Lingiwan went to the spittle of Pagatipanan, and the spittle of Aponigawani went there also; the spittle of Dangdangayan went to the spittle of Pagbokasan and that of Aponibolinayen also, and thus they found out that they were relatives — Pagbokasan was surprised, for he did not know that he had a son, and Ebang took her son and carried him as if he was a baby, while Lingiwan was glad, because he had met his sister during the fight, and Langa-an carried him as if a baby. The heads were put on the sticks around the town; the alan mothers were compelled to attend by the betel-nut which grew on their heads, gave all their things to the sons they had raised, and flew somewhere; and Lingiwan asked his father to make pakdlon for Aponibolinayen, for he wanted to marry her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fay-Cooper Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915), 'Aponibolinayen as Warrior' episodes; not verbatim.
